title: A sock puppet, a Super Bowl and negative gross margins
lede: Pets.com didn’t die because nobody had heard of it. Everybody had. It died because every box it shipped lost money, and the cash ran out before that changed.

chapters.title: An Amazon-backed bet on the pet aisle
chapters.cap: raised privately in 1999 across three preferred stock rounds
chapters.body:
Pets.com was incorporated in California on October 7, 1998. It began operating on February 17, 1999, when it bought the Pets.com domain and a web store from a third party.[^1] An archived page from May 1999 still described the site as “a division of WebMagic™… headed by Greg McLemore.”[^36] Julie Wainwright, who had just been CEO of Reel.com, took over as CEO in March 1999.[^1]

Money arrived fast: a $10.0M Series A in April, a $50.0M Series B in June and another $49.2M in November–December.[^1] Just before the IPO, Amazon.com owned **40.7%** of the company and Hummer Winblad Venture Partners 21.2%.[^1] Headcount went from 4 people in March 1999 to 270 by December.[^1]

The address was older than the company. The .com registry shows pets.com was first registered on Nov 21, 1994, almost four years before Pets.com, Inc. was incorporated.[^54]

chapters.title: The mascot that outlived the company
chapters.cap: spent on marketing & sales for every $1 of revenue in Q4 1999
chapters.body:
TBWA\Chiat\Day[^16] created a wisecracking sock puppet, performed by comedian Michael Ian Black.[^13] It floated as a 36-foot balloon in the 1999 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade[^13], did Good Morning America and Time[^14], and on January 30, 2000 got its own Super Bowl XXXIV spot, a buy widely reported at about $1.2 million.[^16]

Advertising expense alone was **$26.9M** from inception to December 31, 1999[^1]. In Q4 1999, marketing & sales was **$30.7M** against **$5.2M** in net sales.[^2]

chapters.title: Public, four weeks before the top
chapters.cap: IPO price on Feb 11, 2000 (Nasdaq: IPET). The high for the quarter was $14.00
chapters.body:
Merrill Lynch led the sale of 7.5 million shares at $11, raising $82.5M gross and about $75.3M net.[^6] The stock opened at $13½ and was back near $11 by midday. CNET’s headline was “Pets.com IPO is a dog.”[^12]

On March 10 the Nasdaq closed at its all-time bubble high.[^26] The prospectus had already warned that the company might “provide our customers with shipping below our actual costs to attract customers.”[^1]

The offering closed on Feb 16, 2000. Merrill Lynch, Bear Stearns, Thomas Weisel Partners and Warburg Dillon Read were the managing underwriters.[^40]

chapters.title: “Fewer than 8 were even prepared to visit”
chapters.cap: closing price on Nov 7, 2000, down 98% from the IPO price
chapters.body:
Cutting marketing narrowed the losses, from $39.1M in Q1 2000 to $21.7M in Q3. Gross margin improved from −64% to −3% once the Indianapolis-area warehouse took over its share of shipping.[^4] But by September 30 only $23.1M in cash was left.[^4] In July it absorbed rival Petstore.com in an all-stock deal that brought in just $3M of cash.[^7]

Petstore.com, a majority-owned subsidiary of Discovery Communications, was the rival it bought.[^48] Pets.com paid 5,243,752 common shares for its brand, website, customer base, live fish business, supplier agreements and intellectual property, valued at $10.3 million.[^43] The filing priced those shares at $1.8125, the Jul 12 close.[^48] Alongside the deal Discovery bought $3 million of Series A redeemable preferred stock and common stock from Pets.com.[^6]

Merrill Lynch approached more than 50 potential buyers and investors. “Out of the more than 50 prospects contacted, fewer than 8 were even prepared to visit with the company.”[^5] On November 7, 2000, about 255 of the 320 employees were laid off.[^5]

chapters.title: Sold for parts
chapters.cap: total liquidation payout per share, 2001–2004, on an $11 IPO price
chapters.body:
The site stopped taking orders at 11am Pacific on November 9, 2000.[^36] PetSmart.com paid **$375,000** for the domain names and related IP. The sock puppet was explicitly excluded from the deal.[^6] In its December proxy, the board estimated stockholders might receive “up to approximately $0.25 per share.”[^24]

They got less. Three liquidating distributions followed: $0.09 in 2001, $0.075 in 2002 and a final $0.00747 in 2004.[^8][^9][^10]

The estate’s own statements show how fast the books shrank. Net assets in liquidation were $58.7M when liquidation accounting began, $9.6M at Dec 31, 2000 and $4.2M a year later.[^40] Most of the first drop was write-offs: $45.8M of net other expense in the first eight weeks, which included recovering 5,243,752 shares in settlement of an advertising and cross-marketing agreement.[^40] The first two payouts are on the record as paid: $3,128,127 on Sep 28, 2001 and, in September 2002, $2,605,581.[^40][^41]
